title: you already speak a little Yiddish
hookLine: mazel tov, oy vey, schlep: a whole language hiding in English
tomorrow: the plate that tells a story

cards: Mazel tov. Oy vey. Schlep, kvetch, chutzpah, nosh.
Plenty of people say these without a second thought, Jewish or not. They aren't slang.
They're Yiddish, a whole language with its own songs, newspapers and novels, and a lot of English speakers have been using a little of it all along.

teach.b: Yiddish was the everyday language of Ashkenazi Jews in central and eastern Europe for centuries. It's built mostly from old German, with Hebrew and Slavic words mixed in, and it's written in Hebrew letters.
Immigrants carried it to American cities, and English kept a handful.
Schlep: to drag. Kvetch: to complain, at length. Nosh: a little snack.
Chutzpah: nerve, rude or brave depending on who's telling it. Oy vey is short for oy vey iz mir: oh, woe is me.
And mazel tov? Mazel comes from a Hebrew word for a star, and luck; tov means good. Good luck, word for word.
But it isn't said before the exam. It's said after the good news: a birth, a wedding, a new job. It means: a good thing happened.
Then there's the word worth keeping. In German, Mensch just means a person.

teach.h: A MENSCH — A REAL HUMAN BEING.
teach.b: In Yiddish, a mensch is a real human being: decent, honest, someone who does the right thing when nobody's checking.
The great rabbi Hillel taught it long before Yiddish existed: where nobody is acting like a person should, try to be that person.

how: Yiddish is still spoken in some Hasidic communities and is studied and sung widely; many Jews, religious or not, use Yiddish words every day, say mazel tov after good news, and call a decent person a mensch.

games.q: what's inside the words — tap the pairs.

s: Yiddish is a kind of slang
it's a whole language, mostly Germanic, written in Hebrew letters.
mazel tov is said after the good news
it means congratulations: a good thing happened.
in German it's a person; in Yiddish, a decent one.

games.q: a friend calls: she got the job. what's the Yiddish thing to say?
games.why: mazel tov: congratulations, a good thing happened. oy vey is for the other kind of news.

games.q: build it: a star, or luck + good.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: someone you'd call a mensch. Second breath: one thing they did when nobody was checking.
Third breath: let the word land on them, quietly, like a compliment they'll never hear.

wordCard.voice: Mensch. A real human being: decent, honest, there when it counts. Third word.

orig.note: Yiddish, written in Hebrew letters: a person, and in everyday use, a decent, honorable one.

carryVoice: Your line: be a mensch. Of everything Yiddish lent to English, that may be the best one. Day three, done.
